text:
Saskatchewan Court of Appeal

Citation: R. v. Westfair Foods Ltd. and
Canada Safeway Ltd.

Date: 1989-11-08

Docket: 9591 to 9599, both inclusive

Between:

Her Majesty The Queen (appellant)

and

Westfair Foods Ltd., Westfair Drugs
Ltd., Larry Enns, Stewart Postlewaite and Ray Scrutton (respondents) and The
Attorney General of Saskatchewan (intervenor)

And between:

Her Majesty The Queen (appellant)

and

Canada Safeway Limited, Henry
Rolheiser, Scott Dunbar, Mel Genge, Henry Baudais and Larry Thol (respondents)
and The Attorney General of Saskatchewan (intervenor)

Bayda, C.J.S., Cameron and
Sherstobitoff, JJ.A.

Counsel:

W.J. Davern, for the appellant

L. Seiferling and K. Ring, for the respondent,
Westfair Foods et al.

R. Richards and G. Welsch, for the intervenor,
the Attorney General of Saskatchewan

D. Hodson, for the respondent, Canada Safeway
Limited et al.

[
1
]

Cameron,
J.A.: These appeals, which were heard together, concern the constitutionality
of the Province's retail store hours law and the City of Saskatoon's bylaw
regulating retail store hours in the City.

[
2
]

Section
121
of the
Urban Municipality Act, 1984
, S.S. 1983-84, c. U-11 requires
that all retail stores in Saskatchewan, except "convenience" stores
such as confectioneries, service stations and so on, be closed on Sundays and
after 6:00 p.m. on every other day of the week, save Saturday. On Saturday,
they may remain open until 10 p.m. All of this is subject, however, to local
variation. The
Act
empowers urban municipalities, within their
jurisdictions, to vary these closing times and to determine which convenience
stores may remain open, and when, according to their type, size, and location.

[
3
]

Acting
on this power to vary, the City of Saskatoon enacted bylaw 6665 requiring all
retail stores in that City, (except convenience stores of a size not exceeding
1100 square meters) to be closed on Sundays, and after 6:00 p.m. on weekdays,
other than Friday.

[
4
]

The
issue is whether these enactments are inconsistent with the
Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
and more particularly those of its provisions, which
within reasonable and justifiable limits (
s. 1
), guarantee freedom of religion
(
s. 2(a)
) and the right to equality in the law without discrimination (
s. 15
).
If the enactments are inconsistent with the
Charter
in either respect
then a further issue arises: whether they are inoperative generally or only to
the extent of the inconsistency.

[
5
]

In
March and April of 1986, Westfair Foods Ltd. and Westfair Drugs Ltd., which
companies own and operate two SuperValu stores in Saskatoon, were charged under
s. 121(10) of the
Urban Municipality Act
with having breached bylaw 6665
by failing to close their stores on Sundays, contrary to s. 3(1)(e) of the
bylaw, and on Monday evenings, contrary to s. 3(1)(a) of the bylaw. Canada Safeway
Limited, which owns several Safeway stores in Saskatoon, was similarly charged,
as were the managers of these stores.

[
6
]

After
several adjournments, the companies and their store managers appeared in
Provincial Court in Saskatoon on September 2, 1986 before Chief Judge Carey.
They moved on an agreed statement of facts to have the charges quashed on the
ground s. 121 of the
Urban Municipality Act
and ss. 3(1)(e) and 3(1)(a)
of bylaw 6665 were of no force or effect because they were inconsistent with
the
Charter
's
guarantees, first, of freedom of religion and, second, of
the right to equality in the law without discrimination.

[
7
]

Chief
Judge Carey was not satisfied that the enactments, in fact, offended anyone's
freedom of religion, but he was satisfied that the bylaw was unconstitutional
inasmuch as it permitted the opening of some but not all convenience stores,
depending on their size. This, he concluded, was inconsistent with the
constitutional guarantee of equality in the law without discrimination, an inconsistency
which was neither reasonable nor justifiable. Accordingly he held the bylaw in
its entirety to be of no force or effect, and in the result dismissed all the
charges.

[
8
]

The
Crown then appealed to the Court of Queen's Bench. The matter came before Mr.
Justice Wimmer. [See
1987 CanLII 4553 (SK QB)
, 58 Sask. R. 274.] He turned down the appeal on the Sunday
opening charges, but allowed the appeal on the Monday evening charges.

[
9
]

First,
he concluded that the provisions of the law requiring retailers to close on
Sunday violated the constitutional freedom of religion of those retailers whose
Sabbath day is Saturday -- persons of the Jewish and Seventh Day Adventist
faiths -- because the law made it more difficult for them, relative to Sunday
observers, to practice their religious beliefs; they were, in effect, required
to close their stores on both Saturday and Sunday. This, he found, was neither
reasonable nor justifiable.

[
10
]

Second, he concluded that the constitutional guarantee to equality in
the law without discrimination had not been offended. It was his view that the
regulation of business, as such, and the classification of stores that went
with it was beyond the scope of the equality provisions of the
Charter

since those provisions are concerned with affronts to human worth and dignity,
and nothing of that sort was involved in the impugned enactments.

[
11
]

Having come to these conclusions he severed the Sunday closing
provisions from the remainder of the enactments; declared those provisions,
only, to be of no force or effect; quashed the Sunday opening charges; and then
remitted to the Provincial Court for trial those charges having to do with
remaining open Monday evenings.

[
12
]

Both the Crown and the accused then launched appeals to this court.

[
13
]

The Crown appealed on the ground the Sunday closing provisions do not
violate anyone's freedom of religion and that, even if they do, they cannot be
taken to be unenforceable, generally, but only as against those persons whose
freedom of religion they infringe; and since that does not include any of the
accused, the Sunday opening charges, as well as the others, must stand.

[
14
]

The companies and their managers also appealed. They contended that all
the charges must be dismissed for the reason, first, that the Sunday closing
provisions offend freedom of religion and cannot be severed from the rest of
the law and treated as though they, alone, are unenforceable, and second, that
the enactments are inconsistent with the
Charter
's
guarantee of legal
equality and are therefore unenforceable in their entirety.

The Constitutional Provisions At Issue

[
15
]

The sections of the
Charter
and of the
Constitution Act 1982
,
which are in issue, read thus:

"1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable
limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society.

* * * * *

"2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a) freedom of conscience and religion;

* * * * *

"15(1) Every individual is equal before and under the law
and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without
discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race,
national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability.

"(2) Subsection (1) does not preclude any law, program or
activity that has as its object the amelioration of conditions of disadvantaged
individuals or groups including those that are disadvantaged because of race,
national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability.

* * * * *

"24(1) Anyone whose rights or freedoms, as guaranteed by
this
Charter
, have been infringed or denied may apply to a court of competent
jurisdiction to obtain such remedy as the court considers appropriate and just
in the circumstances.

* * * * *

"52(1) The Constitution of Canada is the supreme law of
Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or
effect."

The Impugned Enactments

(a) The Urban Municipality Act 1984

[
16
]

So far as material, s. 121 of this
Act
provides as follows:

"121(1) In this section:

(a) 'closed' means not open for the serving of customers or
the receiving of orders from customers;

(b) 'store' means any building or portion of a building,
booth, stall or other place where goods are exposed or offered for sale or
auction.

"(2) Except as otherwise provided in this section or by a
bylaw passed pursuant to this section, the owner or operator of a store shall ensure
that the store is closed:

(a) on each day from Monday to Friday, inclusive, at 6:00 p.m.
or any earlier hour designated in a bylaw and remains closed until 5:00 a.m. on
the next following day; and

(b) on Saturday at 10:00 p.m. or any earlier hour designated
in a bylaw and remains closed until 5:00 a.m. on the next following Monday.

"(3) A council may, by bylaw, vary the store hours
established by subsection (2) with respect to the whole or any designated part
of the year and with respect to any designated class of stores:

(a) by requiring all such stores to be closed and remain
closed:

(i) at any one of the following times:

(A) during the whole of any one day of the week;

(B) during the afternoon of any one day of the week;

(C) during the afternoon of any one day of the week and before
noon on the next day; or

(D) On Saturday after the hour of noon or later hour that the
council considers appropriate but not later than 10:00 p.m.;

(ii) during the whole or any part of any specified holiday or
any day proclaimed as a civic holiday;

(b) by permitting such stores to remain open until 10:00 p.m.,
or any earlier hour that may be designated in the bylaw, on any one day in each
week and, if that day is a day other than Saturday, requiring those stores to
close on the following Saturday at 6:00 p.m. or at any earlier hour that may be
designated in the bylaw;

(c) by permitting such stores to remain open after 6:00 p.m.
and until the hour designated in the bylaw for not more than 14 specified days
per year in addition to any days permitted pursuant to clause (b).

"(3.1) For the purpose of clause 3(c), the hour
designated in the bylaw until stores are permitted to remain open may be as
late at 5:00 a.m. on the day following the specified day in which case only one
day is deemed to have been specified.

"(4) Neither subsection (2) nor a bylaw passed pursuant
to subsection (3) applies to the owner or operator of a store whose principal
trade or business carried on in the store, as determined by the greatest
percentage of total value of its gross sales, is one of or a combination of:

(a) a tobacconist, that is the sale by retail of tobacco,
cigars, cigarettes and smokers' sundries;

(b) a newsagent, that is the sale by retail of newspapers,
magazines, periodicals, pamphlets, books, writing material, playing cards,
picture cards and souvenirs;

(c) a restaurateur, that is the provision to the public of
prepared food and any drink that may lawfully be sold, for consumption either
on or off the premises, including soft drinks, milk, ice cream and fresh fruit;

(d) a druggist, that is the sale by retail of medicines,
drugs, medical supplies and appliances;

(e) a confectionist, that is the sale by retail of chocolates,
candies, nuts, soft drinks, milk, ice cream and fruit;

(f) a baker, that is the sale by retail of bread, cakes and
pastries;

(g) a milk supplier, that is the sale by retail of any type of
milk and cream;

(h) a garage keeper, that is the provision of repairs to, the
supplying of parts for and the servicing of automobiles and the sale by retail
of petroleum products;

(i) a service station agent, that is the servicing of
automobiles and the sale by retail of petroleum products;

(j) an automobile dealer, that is the sale by retail or
trading of new or used cars;

(k) a greenhouse operator, that is the sale by retail of
plants, produce and related products;

(l) a farm implement dealer, that is the sale by retail or
trading of new or used agricultural implements;

(m) a hotel or motel carrying on one or more of the trades or businesses
mentioned in clause (a) to (l);

and, subject to subsection (5), any such store may sell any or
all of the goods or merchandise that it normally sells or provide any of the
services that it normally provides.

"(5) The council may, by bylaw, with respect to the whole
or any designated part of the year and with respect to all stores mentioned in
subsection (4) or any class of such stores that is designated in the bylaw on
the basis of type, physical size, or location, regulate the hours of opening of
such stores and may restrict the nature of any goods sold or any services
provided in those stores during the hours when other shops are closed pursuant
to subsection (2) or to a bylaw passed pursuant to subsection (3).

"(5.1) Subsections (2) to (5) do not apply to a resort
village unless the council of the resort village passes a bylaw providing that
any or all of those subsections apply to the resort village.

"(6) …

"(7) …

"(8) …

"(9) During the hours when any class of stores in which
goods are offered for sale by retail are required to be closed by this section
or by a bylaw passed pursuant to this section, no goods of the kind ordinarily
sold in stores of that class are to be offered for sale by public auction or by
a transient trader, but this subsection does not apply to used or second-hand
goods.

"(10) When a contravention of any provision of this
section or of a bylaw passed pursuant to this section occurs, the owner or
operator of the store and the person in charge of the store are guilty of an
offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine of not more than $5,000,
and, in the case of a continuing offence, to a further fine of not more than
$250 for each day during which the offence continues and the convicting judge
or justice of the peace shall order that, in default of payment of a fine
imposed pursuant to this subsection, the store in respect of which the offence
took place is to be closed until the fine is paid."

(b) Bylaw 6665

[
17
]

This bylaw, passed pursuant to s. 121 of the
Urban Municipality Act

for the express purpose of regulating store hours in the City of Saskatoon,
provides as follows:

"1. This Bylaw shall be known as 'The Store Hours Bylaw'.

"2. In this Bylaw:

(1) 'Store' means any building or portion of a building,
booth, stall or other place where goods are exposed or offered for sale or
auction;

(2) 'Closed' means not open for the serving of customers or
for the receiving of orders from customers. 'Open' means open for the servicing
of customers or for the receiving of orders from customers;

(3) 'A tobacconist' means the sale by retail of tobacco,
cigars, cigarettes and smokers' sundries;

(4) 'A news agent' means the sale by retail of newspapers,
magazines, periodicals, pamphlets, books, writing material, playing cards,
picture cards and souvenirs;

(5) 'A druggist' means the sale by retail of medicines, drugs,
medical supplies and appliances;

(6) 'A confectionist' means the sale by retail of chocolates,
candies, nuts, soft drinks, milk, ice cream and fruit;

(7) 'A Baker' means the sale by retail of breads, cakes and
pastries;

(8) 'A milk supplier' means the sale by retail of any type of
milk or cream;

(9) 'A service station agent' means the servicing of
automobiles and the sale by retail of petroleum products;

(10) 'Holiday' means New Year's Day, Good Friday, Victoria
Day, Dominion Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving Day, Remembrance Day and Christmas
Day. Should any of these holidays fall on a Sunday, then the day following
shall be such holiday. Holiday also includes any day proclaimed as a holiday by
either the Governor-General or the Lieutenant-Governor.

(11) 'Size' means the area in square metres where goods are
offered for sale or displayed for sale.

"3(1) Except as otherwise provided in Section 4, all
stores shall be closed:

a. on a Monday that is not a holiday from 6:00 p.m. until 5:00
a.m. the next day.

b. on a Tuesday that is not a holiday, from 6:00 p.m. until
5:00 a.m. the next day.

c. on a Wednesday that is not a holiday from 6:00 p.m. until
5:00 a.m. the next day.

d. on a Thursday that is not a holiday from 10:00 p.m. until
5:00 a.m. the next day.

e. on a Saturday that is not a holiday from 6:00 p.m. until
5:00 a.m. the next following Monday.

"(2) Except as otherwise provided in Section 4, all
stores shall be closed on a holiday from 5:00 a.m. until 5:00 a.m. the next
day.

"4(1) A store that is of a size of 1,100 square metres or
less
and
in which the principal trade or business carried on in the
store, as determined by the greatest percentage of total value of its gross
sales, is one of, or a combination of:

(a) a tobacconist,

(b) a news agent,

(c) a druggist,

(d) a confectionist,

(e) a baker,

(f) a milk supplier,

shall be closed every day from 1:00 a.m. to 5:00 a.m.

"(2) A store in which the principal trade of business
carried on in the store, as determined by the greatest percentage of total
value of its gross sales, is that of a service station agent may remain open
during all hours.

"(3) A store that is of a size of 250 square metres or
less and in which the principal trade or business carried on in the store, as
determined by the greatest percentage of total value of its gross sales, is a
combination of a service station agent
and
one or more of:

(a) a tobacconist,

(b) a news agent,

(c) a druggist,

(d) a confectionist,

(e) a baker,

(f) a milk supplier

may be open during all hours."

The Questions At Issue

1. Are s. 121(2)(b) of the
Urban Municipality Act 1984

and s. 3(1)(e) of bylaw 6665 of the City of Saskatoon (the Sunday closing
provisions), inconsistent with
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
?

2. If so, are they saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
as
constituting reasonable and demonstrably justifiable limits on the freedom of
religion of those whose Sabbath is Saturday?

3. If not, are these provisions of no force or effect
generally, or only to the extent they affect Saturday-observing retailers?

4. Are either of the enactments, by reason of their
classifications, inconsistent with
s. 15
of the
Charter
?

5. If either enactment is inconsistent with s. 15, is it saved
by s. 1?

6. If not, to what extent is the enactment of no force or
effect?

1. Are The Sunday Closing Provisions Inconsistent With Freedom Of Religion?

[
18
]

In answering this question in the affirmative, Mr. Justice Wimmer relied
upon the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Edwards Books and
Art Ltd.
,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713; 71 N.R. 161; 19 O.A.C. 239; 30 C.C.C.(3d)
385; 55 C.R.(3d) 193. That case concerned charges brought against four Ontario
retailers for conducting business on Sunday in contravention of the Ontario
Retail
Business Holidays Act.
One of those charged was Nortown Foods Limited whose
two shareholders were of the Jewish faith.

[
19
]

The court held, first, that the statute was within the power of the
Province to enact and had not been enacted for the religious purpose of
encouraging worship on Sundays. Had that been its purpose, the court would have
rendered the statute unconstitutional, but as it was the court was satisfied
that the law had been enacted for the valid secular purpose of providing
uniform holidays or common days of pause for those engaged in retail work.

[
20
]

Second, the majority of the court held that the
Act
infringed the
s. 2(a) religious freedom of those whose Sabbath day was Saturday, including
persons of the Jewish and Seventh Day Adventist faiths. It did so for the
reason, primarily, that the effect of the
Act
was to impose upon
Saturday observing retailers the disadvantage of having to remain closed an
extra day relative to Sunday observing retailers, thus making it more difficult
for the Saturday observer to manifest or practice his or her religious beliefs.

[
21
]

Mr. Justice Wimmer, following the lead of
Edward Books
,
considered, first, the purpose of the impugned enactments, then their effects.
He said this:

"There is nothing in the text of s. 121 of the
Urban
Municipality Act
or of the
Store Hours Bylaw
to indicate that either
was enacted as part of a scheme to promote Sunday as a day of religious
observance. Nor is there any evidence to suggest that such was the case. Both
enactments deal with the closing hours of retail stores on all days, including
Sundays, and I am persuaded that insofar as Sunday closing is concerned their
purpose is to provide a common day away from work for retail employees. I
conclude, therefore, that both enactments have a valid purpose. But what of
their effects?

"In
R. v. Edwards Books
there was evidence on
record that those of the Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist faiths in Ontario
observe Saturday as their Sabbath. This evidence provided a footing for the
conclusion that the Ontario statute runs foul of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

There is no similar evidence in this case concerning the religious observances
of those in Saskatchewan professing the same faiths. However, I do not think
that the absence of such evidence would be a sound reason for holding that the
Sunday closing requirements of the
Act
and the bylaw do not also run
foul of s. 2(a).

"In
Jones v. The Queen
(1987),
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, 69 N.R. 241; 25
C.R.R. 63, LaForest, J., made the following observation at page 74:

'A court must be taken to have a general knowledge of our
history and values and to know at least the broad design and workings of our
society.'

"It is true he was speaking in the context of an inquiry
to determine whether a certain statutory violation of the appellant's freedom
of religion could be justified. Nevertheless, I think the same observation can
apply when examining the purpose and effects of legislation in
Charter

cases. This is especially so when a court is required by
s. 27
of the
Charter

to recognize the multicultural heritage of Canadians. To me it would seem an
act of judicial blindness not to recognize that there are in the City of
Saskatoon, in the Province of Saskatchewan, persons of the Jewish and
Seventh-day Adventist faiths whose religious day of rest is Saturday and, as
well, that some of those persons are engaged in retail trades.

"The Ontario statute was found to impact adversely upon
the freedom of Saturday observers in that province to practice their religious
beliefs. In my opinion, the Sunday closing provisions of the
Urban
Municipality Act, 1984
and the
Store Hours Bylaw
have the same
impact upon Saturday observers in Saskatchewan and thus infringe upon the
freedom guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.
"

[
22
]

Assuming the existence in Saskatoon of retailers of the Jewish or
Seventh Day Adventists faiths who for religious reasons remain closed on
Saturdays, we find ourselves in respectful agreement with Mr. Justice Wimmer's
analysis and with his conclusion.

[
23
]

That then shifts the issue to
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

2. Are The Sunday Closing Provisions, Though They Violate Freedom Of
Religion, Saved By S. 1 Of The Charter?

[
24
]

Mr. Justice Wimmer concluded they were not, saying:

"The rights and freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter

are not without limit.
Section 1
of the
Charter
subjects them '… to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free
and democratic society.'.

"In
R. v. Edwards Books
, Chief Justice Dickson
described at page 768 what is required to meet the test implicit in s. 1:

'Two requirements must be satisfied to establish that a limit
is reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
First, the legislative objective which the limitation is designed to promote
must be of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a constitutional right.
It must bear on a "pressing and substantial concern". Second, the
means chosen to attain those objectives must be proportional or appropriate to
the ends. The proportionality requirement, in turn, normally has three aspects:
the limiting measures must be carefully designed, or rationally connected, to
the objective; they must impair the right as little as possible; and their
effects must not so severely trench on individual or group rights that the
legislative objective, albeit important, is nevertheless outweighed by the
abridgment of rights.'

"These requirements were first enunciated by the Supreme
Court in
R. v. Oakes
,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103; 65 N.R. 87; 14 O.A.C. 335; 50
C.R.(3d) 1; 24 C.C.C.(3d) 321; 26 D.L.R.(4th) 200. The Ontario statute was
found to have met the test. It is unnecessary for me to reiterate the reasons
given beyond saying that the Court viewed the objective of a common pause day
for workers as a matter of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a
constitutional right, and considered the limiting measures to be rationally
connected to the objective and designed to abridge the freedom of religion of
Saturday observers as little as possible. It is on the last point that a
comparison of the Ontario and Saskatchewan positions break down.

"The Ontario statute contains a Sabbatarian exemption for
Saturday observing retailers. It exempts from its Sunday closing requirements
those retail stores which were closed on the previous day, provided not more
than seven people are employed in the store on Sunday and provided the store
area used on Sunday does not exceed 5000 square feet. This exemption persuaded
Chief Justice Dickson and those who concurred in his judgment that a
satisfactory legislative effort had been made to mitigate any infringement of
freedom of religion. It seems that the Chief Justice would not have found the
statute to be valid in the absence of some such exemption. At page 782 he
stated:

'In my view, the principles articulated in
Oakes
make
it incumbent on a legislature which enacts Sunday closing laws to attempt very
seriously to alleviate the effects of those laws on Saturday observers. The
exemption in S. 3(4) of the
Act
under review in these appeals represents
a satisfactory effort on the part of the Legislature of Ontario to that end and
is, accordingly, permissible.'

"Neither the Legislature of Saskatchewan nor the
municipal council of the City of Saskatoon made any attempt to alleviate the
effects of their laws on Saturday observers and that omission, it appears, is
fatal.

"In the result, I find that the Sunday closing provisions
contained in the
Urban Municipality Act, 1984
and in the
Store Hours
Bylaw
do infringe
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and that the infringement
is not justifiable under s. 1."

[
25
]

It might be noted that following this decision the Legislature enacted a
Sabbatarian exemption (Bill 37, assented to September 15, 1987). The validity
of the charges in issue
in this case
, however, falls to be determined in
the absence of such an exemption.

[
26
]

We are inclined to agree with Mr. Justice Wimmer, but find it
unnecessary in light of what follows to express a final view on this aspect of
the matter. For the purpose of advancing the analysis, however, we shall take
it that the impugned measures to not meet the s. 1 tests of
Oakes
by
reason of the absence of a Sabbatarian exemption.

[
27
]

That then brings us to the third of the s. 2(a) questions.

3. Are The Sunday Closing Provisions Of No Force Or Effect Generally Or
Only To The Extent They Infringe The Religious Freedom Of Saturday Observing
Retailers Who, For Religious Reasons, Remain Closed On Saturdays?

[
28
]

Mr. Justice Wimmer decided that the law had to be taken to be wholly
unenforceable. The alternative, which amounts in effect to granting Saturday
observing retailers a constitutional exemption, was in his view fraught with
too many difficulties. He said this:

"Insofar as certainty in the law is possible, it is
desirable. To cast legislation in broad terms with the understanding that it
may be limited in its application would be to promote uncertainty. For example,
in the circumstances of these appeals who would be entitled to claim a
constitutional exemption? Would an exemption be available to all Saturday
observing retailers or only to those who actually close their establishments on
Saturdays for religious reasons? Would a corporation -- which cannot express a religious
preference -- be denied an exemption even if all of its shareholders were
Sabbatarians? This list of uncertainties is by no means closed.

"Also, every claim of exemption would involve an inquiry
into a person's religious beliefs, either by administrative officials, law
enforcement officers or courts, and often by all three. Official inquiries into
such matter may be demeaning and offensive and they are undesirable. Such
inquiries themselves might constitute a
Charter
violation.

"Finally, the enforcement of a law applicable to some and
not others might encounter obstacles arising from the equality rights set out
in
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

"The problem of fashioning the law to suit the
Constitution is for the legislators, not the courts.

"Therefore, I conclude that the Sunday closing provisions
which are the subject of these appeals are of no force or effect."

[
29
]

This was said by counsel for the Attorney General and the Crown to be an
unnecessary, excessive, and unrealistic response, beyond the power of the
court; unnecessary because each of the difficulties identified by Mr. Justice
Wimmer could be overcome; excessive, for the law offended the constitution in
only a comparatively minor way; unrealistic, since if the courts were to take
this approach generally, few laws could survive; and beyond the power of the
court, because s. 52(1) empowers the courts to declare unenforceable a law
which is inconsistent with the constitution but only "to the extent of the
inconsistency".

[
30
]

As for the first of these submissions, it should be noted at the outset
that the difficulties identified by Mr. Justice Wimmer do not
necessarily

stand in the way of holding the law to be unenforceable only as against
Saturday-observing retailers. Two, only, of the three sources of difficulty to
which he referred could arguably bar such a remedy: the inquiry into a person's
religious beliefs, and the enforcement of the law against some but not others.
If either were by law prohibited that would put an end to the exemption as an
alternative. With respect, however, we do not think that to be the case.

[
31
]

Chief Justice Dickson said in
Edwards Books
(at p. 780):

"I do not mean to suggest that a judicial inquiry into
the sincerity of religious beliefs is unconstitutional. To so hold would mean that
the courts could never grant constitutional exemptions from legislation which
impinged on the free exercise of religious beliefs. Judicial inquiries into
religious beliefs are largely unavoidable if the constitutional freedoms
guaranteed by s. 2(a) are to be asserted before the courts. We must live with
the reality that such an inquiry is necessary in order for the same values to
be given effect by the judicial system. Inquiries which are genuinely designed
as a means of giving effect to religious freedoms will not therefore generally
be unconstitutional. There will, however, be occasions when a substantial
measure of religious feeedom can be achieved without mandating a
state-conducted inquiry into personal religious convictions and the
legislatures ought to be encouraged to do so, if a fair balance is
struck."

We respectfully agree with this observation, and do not think
inquiries of the kind alluded to by Mr. Justice Wimmer would be
unconstitutional if undertaken genuinely for the purpose of giving effect to
the religious freedom guaranteed by the
Charter
.

[
32
]

Nor, to turn to the second of the difficulties to which he referred, do
we think s. 15 operates as a bar. The section does not require that the law
always treat persons the same, but that they be treated as equals, deserving of
equal respect and consideration. As Chief Justice Dickson observed in
R. v.
Big M Drug Mart

1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985], 1 S.C.R. 295; [1985] 3 W.W.R. 481; 58 N.R. 81; 60
A.R. 161; 18 C.C.C.(3d) 305; 18 D.L.R.(4th) 321 (p. 347), "The interest of
true equality may well require differentiation in treatment." An exemption
in favour of the limited class under consideration, to permit members of that
class to manifest and practice their religious beliefs with no disadvantage
relative to the class of Sunday-observing retailers, is consistent with
treating both classes of retailers with equal regard. In principle, therefore,
s. 15 does not stand in the way of recognizing an exemption.

[
33
]

That leaves for consideration the uncertainties about who, more
precisely, might be entitled to an exemption should the law be taken to be
unenforceable only as against Saturday-observing retailers. To be sure, this
presents some difficulty. While the courts can address, generally, the
constitutional principles underlying the matter, they are in no position to law
down comprehensive guidelines. Even to the limited extent that might be
possible and appropriate, it would be quite unwise. And policy formulation, as
Mr. Justice Wimmer noted, is for the legislature.

[
34
]

That is not to say, however, that some useful statement of general
principle cannot be made, for it can. The general principle underlying this
issue is that the practice of one's religion and the manifestation of one's
religious beliefs is not, on account of government action, to be made more or
less easy depending upon whether one is a Saturday or a Sunday observer. The
purpose therefore of an exemption would be to ensure that those persons who,
out of religious conviction, keep holy Saturday, rather than Sunday, are not placed
at a disadvantage. With that in mind, it may be said that those persons who for
religious reasons closed their stores on Saturday would be entitled to open
them on Sunday. But they could not remain open both days any more than could a
Sunday-observer.

[
35
]

Although that leaves much to be answered, we cannot go further. Thus, as
Mr. Justice Wimmer suggested, the recognition of an exemption, in order to
uphold the law generally, is not an entirely satisfactory response. But then
neither is the alternative. It, too, is fraught with difficulties. And they
cannot be overlooked.

[
36
]

The alternative is to bring down the Sunday closing provisions in their
entirety, even though constitutionally their purposes are wholly valid and
their effects for the most part are unassailable. Immediately, that appears
excessive and unrealistic.

[
37
]

To repeat, we are not here dealing with a law whose
purpose
is
unconstitutional; only its
effects
, in comparatively small measure, are
so. To regard as altogether inoperative a law which in purpose or universal
effect is inconsistent with the constitution is readily understandable; an
unconstitutional purpose reaches across the whole of the law. But to regard as
wholly inoperative a law which in incidental effect, only, is inconsistent with
the constitution begs explanation.

[
38
]

If, as a general matter, laws of that nature were to be brought down,
much of the law could not survive, for in the full range of their effects many
laws touch adversely upon the rights and freedoms of the
Charter
.
Such
an approach would therefore be unrealistic.

[
39
]

It would, as well, be destructive of mutual respect between the
legislative and judicial branches of government -- a point needing little
elaboration, but see Professor Gibsons' article
Accentuating the Positive
and Eliminating the Negative: Remedies
…, appearing at p. 311 of
Righting
The Balance; Canada's New Equality Rights.

[
40
]

Nor is it necessary to the full protection of the rights and freedoms of
the
Charter
that such an approach be taken. Individual remedies granted pursuant
to s. 24(1) can protect rights and freedoms adequately by dealing discretely
and precisely with those situations where the effect of an otherwise valid law
impinges a right or freedom. This was the view taken by the majority of this
court in
Reference Re French Language Rights
,
1987 CanLII 204 (SK CA)
, [1987] 5 W.W.R. 577; 58
Sask. R. 161.

[
41
]

Moreover, and this is especially important, the court's power to render
inoperative the whole of the law, not just its offending effects, is highly
questionable in light of the language of s. 52(1). That section provides that
any law which is inconsistent with the constitution is "to the extent of
the inconsistency" of no force or effect. It should perhaps be noted that
the section not only
empowers
the courts to act, but imposes upon them a

duty
to do so:
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
There Chief Justice
Dickson, at p. 353 said of s. 52(1):

"If a court or tribunal finds any statute to be
inconsistent with the Constitution, the overriding effect of the
Charter
,
s.
52(1)
, is to give the court not only the power, but the duty, to regard the
inconsistent statute, to the extent of the inconsistency, as being no longer
'of force or effect'."

[
42
]

Even if the power of a court applying s. 52(1) should extend beyond its
duty, it is our view that where the inconsistency exists neither in purpose nor
in universal effect, and there exists a viable way to confine the extent of the
invalidity, then it is incumbent upon the court to so confine it.

[
43
]

This is the practice in the United States. Professor Tribe, in
American
Constitutional Law
(New York: The Foundation Press Inc., 1978), at pp.
7120-7121, summarizes the practice thus:

"Of course, almost every law … is potentially applicable
to constitutionally protected acts; that danger is not ordinarily thought to
invalidate the law as such but merely to invalidate its enforcement against
protected activity. A plausible challenge to a law as
void for overbreadth

can be made only when (1) the protected activity is a significant part of the
law's target, and (2) there exists no satisfactory way of severing the law's
constitutional from its unconstitutional applications so as to excise the
latter clearly in a single step from the law's reach."

See, too,
R. v. Seaboyer and Gayne
(1987),
1987 CanLII 174 (ON CA)
, 20 O.A.C. 345;
58 C.R.(2d) 289 (Ont. C.A.).

[
44
]

In light of these considerations, we have concluded that, even if it
were within the power of the court to render the Sunday-closing provisions of
no force or effect whatever, it would be inappropriate to do so. Of the two
remedies, the exemption, even with its uncertainties, appears to us to be
preferable.

[
45
]

For these reasons we find ourselves unable, with the greatest of
respect, to agree with Mr. Justice Wimmer on this aspect of his decision. We
believe the Sunday closing provisions of the enactments are subject to being
rendered inoperative only to the extent they violate the religious freedom of
those retailers who in fact, for religious reasons, close their stores on
Saturday. Thus, the position of the accused on this limb of their case must
fail.

[
46
]

Before going further, we should, perhaps, add that we are not invited to
consider, (nor have we considered) the effect of the impugned provisions on
other than Saturday-observing retailers. Nor, of course, have we yet considered
whether, and to what extent, the Sunday closing provisions may or may not be
enforceable in the light of s. 15(1). That, of course, is another issue
altogether. And it is to that issue we now turn.

4. Are Either Of The Enactments, By Reason Of Their Classifications,
Inconsistent With S. 15 Of The Charter?

[
47
]

Counsel for the accused contended that each of the
Act
and bylaw
are inconsistent with
s. 15
of the
Charter
because they treat persons
differently and unequally. This they do in three ways:

First: Persons engaged in retail business are treated
differently and adversely relative to persons engaged in other forms of
enterprise or business, inasmuch as retailers, alone, are singled out for
regulation: the wholesale, manufacturing, and service industries, for example,
are free of regulation, and persons carrying on businesses of that nature may
remain open every day of the week and at all hours.

Second: Retailers are classified by reference to, and treated
more or less favourably depending upon, the kinds of goods they sell: those
selling cars or machinery, for example, are permitted by the
Act
to
remain open, while those selling fridges and stoves must close; and the bylaw
allows persons selling drugs to open while requiring those who sell clothing to
close.

Third: Retailers are subject (in the case of the
Act
)
and subjected (in the case of the bylaw) to different, and more or less
favourable treatment, according to the size of their businesses: only those
whose stores exceed 1100 square meters in size are forced by the bylaw to close
on Sundays and at other times.

[
48
]

These classifications were not said to violate the constitutional rights
of Westfair or Safeway -- as corporations they did not claim to have s. 15
rights to equality in the law. Instead, it was said that the classifications
were generally inconsistent with s. 15, that in consequence the impugned
measures were of no force or effect whatsoever (s. 52(1)), and that the
enactments could not, therefore, ground a charge against anyone, including a
corporation:
R. v. Big M. Drug Mart Ltd.

[
49
]

The Crown and the Attorney General took issue with that position on the
primary ground the
Act
and the bylaw do no more than regulate business
and as such lie outside the reach of s. 15. It was said the enactments are
wholly unconnected to the sections' concerns about the human worth and dignity
of the individual because all they do is classify stores with reference to such
commercial features as whether they are "retail stores" or
"exempt stores" or stores or of a certain "store size".

[
50
]

Wimmer, J., having considered the s. 15 approaches taken by this court
in
Reference re French Language Rights
, concluded that the
classifications were, indeed, beyond the scope of s. 15:

"The forms of equality guaranteed by s. 15(1) and the
forms of inequality forbidden, are those connected to human rights concepts of
individual worth and dignity. The regulation of businesses per se is not so
connected and is not governed by s. 15 in the absence of some trespass against
human right rights objectives. I do not think the section has any application
to the circumstances presented here."

[
51
]

Sometime after Mr. Justice Wimmer rendered his decision, and while the
appeal, having been argued, was in reserve in this court, the Supreme Court of
Canada rendered its decisions in
Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia
,

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 W.W.R. 289; [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143; 91 N.R. 255 (S.C.C.) and
R. v.
Turpin
(1989),
1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
, 96 N.R. 115; 34 O.A.C. 115; 69 C.R.(3d) 97. These are now
the controlling authorities on the application of
s. 15
of the
Charter
.

[
52
]

The Supreme Court formulated a three stepped approach to determining
whether a legislative enactment violates the
Charter
's
equality
provisions. As summarized in this court's reasons for judgment in
R. v. S.B.
and H.B.
(1989),
1989 CanLII 4802 (SK CA)
, 76 Sask. R. 308 (July 11, 1989), the steps are these:

1. The first [step] addresses whether the impugned legislation
denies to the individual any of his or her four basic equality rights under s.
15.

2. The second addresses whether the equality right found to be
denied was denied with discrimination on grounds relating to the personal
characteristics of the individual or of the group to which he or she belongs.

3. The third addresses whether the violation of s. 15, if that
should be found, is justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

[
53
]

Ordinarily we would work our way through the issues progressively, step
by step, but in the circumstances we have decided not to do that. The Supreme
Court's decisions in
Andrews
and
Turpin
came down after the
hearing of this appeal and counsel have not had the opportunity to address
these issues in light of those decisions. Moreover, the case can be fully
resolved at the third step -- which counsel were able to argue fully. We have
decided therefore to proceed immediately to that step. In other words, we shall
put the case for the accused at its highest at this juncture by assuming,
without deciding, that the impugned provisions operate to deprive individuals
of one or more of their s. 15 equality rights and that they do so on such
ground as consititutes discrimination. That then moves the issues to s. 1:
whether there exists sufficient justification to save the impugned provisions.

[
54
]

Before addressing that issue, we should like to say that we are inclined
to agree with Mr. Justice Wimmer's conclusion. Even if the impugned enactments
could be said to have violated one or more of the equality rights enshrined in
s. 15(1), it would have been difficult in our view to have concluded that the
violation was discriminatory having regard for the Supreme Court's definition
of "discrimination". Having said that, however, and having made the
assumptions we have for the purpose of moving the case on to ground that was
fully argued, we turn to the fifth question, involving the application of step
three of the approach formulated by the Supreme Court.

5. Assuming Either Enactment Is Inconsistent With S. 15, Is It Saved By S.
1?

[
55
]

This depends on two things: First, the objectives of the enactments must
be of sufficient importance to warrant the overriding of s. 15. Second, the
means chosen to achieve the objectives must be appropriate to the ends:
R.
v. Oakes
.

(1) Objects And Means

[
56
]

The enactments are intended to ensure that people who earn their
livelihoods in the retail sector have periods of leisure in common with others,
especially family and friends, so that activities of a family, social, and
recreational kind may be shared. Thus, on Sundays, holidays, and most evenings,
all retailers must cease conducting business. All, that is, except for those
who provide goods and services of necessity or convenience. This exception was
created for the obvious reason that the value of the common pause times would
be diminished if things like drugs, magazines, basic foods stuffs, gasoline,
and the like were not available during these times.

[
57
]

The means chosen to achieve these objects consists of the three
classifications earlier referred to: that between retailers and wholesalers;
that between retailers selling one kind of good or service and those selling another
kind; and that between retailers who trade out of larger premises and those who
trade out of smaller premises.

(2) The Objects And Their Importance

[
58
]

We are of the opinion the objective -- ensuring common pause times for
working people -- is of sufficient importance to warrant such s. 15 override as
this case presents.

[
59
]

The
Edwards Books
case raised a similar issue. There Chief
Justice Dickson had little difficulty finding that the social objective of the
Ontario counterpart of the enactments before us was of such substantial and
pressing kind as to warrant overriding a
Charter
provision. He said (p.
770):

"I regard as self-evident the desirability of enabling
parents to have regular days off from work in common with their child's day off
from school, and with a day off enjoyed by most other family and community
members. I reiterate the view exposed in
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
, at p.
353:

'I accept the secular justification for a day of rest in a
Canadian context and the reasonableness of a day of rest has been clearly
enunciated by the courts in the United States of America.'

"A family visit to an uncle or a grandmother, the
attendance of a parent at a child's sports tournament, a picnic, a swim, or a
hike in the park on a summer day, or a family expedition to a zoo, circus, or
exhibition -- these, and hundreds of other leisure activities with family and
friends are amongst the simplest but most profound joys that any of us can
know. The aim of protecting workers, families and communities from a diminution
of opportunity to experience the fulfillment offered by these activities, and
from the alienation of the individual from his or her closest social bonds, is
not one which I regard as unimportant or trivial. In the context of the
'fast-growing trend toward wide-scale store openings' (Report, p. 267), I am
satisfied that the
Act
is aimed at a pressing and substantial concern.
It therefore survives the first part of the inquiry under s. 1."

[
60
]

The Chief Justice's reference to a "Report", was to the
Report
On Sunday Observance Legislation
: Ontario Law Reform Commission (1970).
That Report was introduced into evidence in the present case as well, and
though it is of limited value here, it does show what prompts governments to
want to preserve common pause times.

[
61
]

We are satisfied, then, that the first limb of the s. 1 issue has been
satisfied.

(3) The Means Chosen To Achieve The Objectives

[
62
]

The essential question here is whether in seeking to attain the social
objective of securing common pause times the enactments have struck a
reasonable and fair balance between, on the one hand, the interests of society
generally and, on the other, the interests of those persons adversely affected
by the laws' classifications. That entails considering, first, whether the
objective and the means chosen to achieve it are rationally connected; second,
whether the classifications impair as little as possible the constitutional
entitlement of those persons to equality in the law; and, third, whether the
effects of the classifications remain reasonably proportionate to the
objective:
R. v. Oakes
.

(i) The Connection Between The Objective And The Means

(a) Retailers v. Non-Retailers

[
63
]

Counsel for the Attorney General submitted, and we agree with him, that
there are obvious and compelling reasons why s. 121 of the
Urban
Municipality Act
regulates only retailers. The retail end of business is
more ubiquitous, and those engaged in that end of it have a great propensity to
conduct commercial activity on all days and at all hours than do those engaged
in the manufacturing and wholesale ends of business. That is true, too, of the
retail sector compared with the service sector. As counsel for the Attorney
General aptly put it, the retailing of goods, especially, "is the most
visible face of commercial activity" and its operations "have a major
impact on the flavour and quality of pause times". This is so not only
because of the number of persons employed in retail businesses but because of
the number of persons who patronize them. And, since the non-retail aspects of
sectors have traditionally shown little tendency to conduct business in the
evenings and on Sundays, there has been no pressing need to directly regulate
their operations during these times: See
Edwards Books
(pp. 747-48) and
the agreed statement of facts in this case (paras. 8, 9 and 10).

[
64
]

In
Edwards Books
Chief Justice Dickson (at p. 771) said:

"I have already referred to the perception of the Law
Reform Commission that the retail industry presented a particularly pressing
problem. It was in this industry that the Report told of competitive pressures
forcing individual operators to extend their hours of business, largely against
their wishes. The Report also documented the characteristics of the retail
trade's labour force, including its low level of unionization, its high
proportion of women, and its generally heterogeneous composition: p. 103. The
Commission's conclusion that this labour force was especially vulnerable to
subtle and overt pressure from its employers amply justified on the evidence
the legislature's decision to single out the retail industry for special and
immediate attention."

[
65
]

We are satisfied that similar considerations underlie the legislative
purpose in enacting s. 121 of the
Urban Municipality Act
, and we have no
difficulty in concluding that there exists a rational connection between the
objectives of the enactments and the first of their classifications. It cannot
be said this classification is arbitrary or unfair or irrational.

(b) Exempt v. Non-Exempt Retailers

[
66
]

This is the second of the law's classifications. Some retailers may
remain open while others are forced to close. The businesses of retailers who
may remain open during common pause times share this trait: they offer goods
and services of necessity or convenience without which, as we said earlier, the
common pause times would suffer. Having regard for the attitudes and habits of
contemporary society, it is essential to the social objective at issue that
classifications of this nature be made. That is their connection to the
objective, and it is, in our view, a rational connection.

[
67
]

Similar exemptions were found acceptable to the Supreme Court in
Edwards
Books
(pp. 771-72). Not unimportantly the Chief Justice observed (at p.
772).

"In drafting its statute, the legislature can, if it
wishes, create categories of retail businesses which are exempted, even though
some un-exempted businesses may sell some of the same products. Legislative
choices regarding alternative forms of business regulations do not generally
impinge on the values and provisions of the
Charter
, and the resultant
legislation need not be tuned with great precision in order to withstand
judicial scrutiny. Simplicity and administrative convenience are legitimate
concerns for the drafters of such legislation."

[
68
]

We should perhaps pause here to say that we have approached this
classification generally, rather than specifically. We have not considered, for
example, whether allowing one person to sell a car on Sunday while prohibiting
another from selling a fridge (s. 121(4)(j) of the
Act
) is rationally
connected to the objective. And we must not be taken to have passed on matters
that specific. Someone attacking a particular aspect of this classification may
or may not be able to make out a case for relief; we are not concerned with
that. We are saying that in the context of this case, which does not require
more, this classification between persons entitled to remain open and those
having to close is, in general, appropriately connected to the social objective
in issue.

(c) Store Size

[
69
]

In this respect, the
Act
and the bylaw must be considered
separately.

[
70
]

Section 121(5) enables an urban council to classify convenience stores
by reference to "physical size", to regulate the hours of such
stores, and to determine the nature of the goods or services which during off
hours may be offered for sale in stores of that kind.

[
71
]

The rationale for
some
size-based regulation is obvious. It is to
permit local councils to better determine the nature of the commercial
environment which in their communities will be permitted to exist during pause
periods. Were it not for this or some similar power, single stores, by
combining the various "exempt" categories of operation, could conduct
major operations during pause times thus frustrating the purpose of the scheme:
See
Edwards Books
, pp. 777-778.

[
72
]

That being the case, we are satisfied, so far as the
Act
is
concerned, that this enabling provision is rationally related to the objective.

[
73
]

As for the bylaw, it classifies convenience stores according to whether
they exceed 1100 square meters in size. Why the City of Saskatoon chose this
standard we cannot know. We do know, however, that were it not for the bylaw's
requirement that retailers whose store size exceeds 1100 square meters close on
Sundays and in the evenings, then the Westfair companies and Safeway could
remain open at these times (See agreed statement of facts especially para. 5).
Given their size (they are major retail operations, not corner stores) were
they to remain open during these times, the objective of the bylaw would to
that extent be defeated.

[
74
]

The difficulty here is knowing whether 1100 square meters is reasonably
related to the purpose of the bylaw. Neither side offered anything concrete by
which that might be judged. How, then, are we to know whether this is
appropriate? This being an attack, generally, on the constitutionality of the
law as opposed to a specific attack by a specific individual adversely affected
by it, we are inclined to fall back onto Chief Justice Dickson's observations
in
Edwards Books
: that legislative choices of this kind do not generally
touch upon the values protected by the
Charter
, and thus

"… the resultant legislation need not be tuned with great
precision in order to withstand judicial scrutiny. Simplicity and
administrative convenience are legitimate concerns for the drafters of such
legislation."

In the circumstances, and having regard for our view that
classifying with reference to store size is
generally
appropriate, we
are not prepared to collapse the bylaw on this ground.

[
75
]

We find a measure of support for this view in some additional comments
of the Chief Justice in
Edwards Books
(p. 781-782). In considering the
propriety of an exemption based on the number of employees, he said he did not
believe

"… there is any magic in the number seven as distinct
from, say, five, ten, or fifteen employees as the cut-off point for eligibility
for the exemption. In balancing the interests of retail employees to a holiday
in common with their family and friends against the s. 2(a) interests of those
affected the Legislature engaged in the process envisaged by
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

A 'reasonable limit' is one which, having regard for the principles enunciated
in Oakes, it was reasonable for the legislature to impose.
The courts are
not called upon to substitute judicial opinions for legislative ones as to the
place at which to draw a precise line.
"

(emphasis added)

[
76
]

With that we may move on to consider the remaining components of the s.
1 tests for justification, namely whether the classifications impair as little
as possible the legal equality rights in issue, and whether their effects
remain reasonable proportionate to the social objectives of the enactments.
These additional considerations will be dealt with together.

(ii) Additional Considerations

[
77
]

In commenting upon the way in which s. 1 falls to be applied, the Chief
Justice in
Edwards Books
noted (p. 769) that the Supreme Court has been
careful to avoid rigid and inflexible standards, recognizing that "the
nature of the proportionality test would vary depending on the
circumstances". Having regard for this, and for the approach taken by the
majority of this court in
Reference Re French Language Rights
, we are of
the view that the contexts in which legal distinctions arise -- the interests
they affect, the basis for their making, and the way in which they touch those
interests -- bear upon the proportionality issue.

[
78
]

Here the interest is economic freedom, and the classifications rest on
impersonal, commercial grounds. Obviously this makes justification easier.

[
79
]

Moreover, it is not as though any of those persons affected by the
impugned classifications has had his or her ability to function freely in the
market place abrogated or even crippled relative to others. The laws do not
abrogate, they regulate. And they regulate minimally. They only curtail
commercial activity on one day of the week, in the evenings and overnight, and
on a limited number of holidays. And even then, a considerable measure of
flexibility is permitted. The
Act
allows council to permit some evening
store openings until 10:00 p.m. (See especially the
Urban Municipality
Amendment Act, 1986
, (No. 2),
S.S. 1986, c. 38
). And the bylaw permits
retailers to remain open all night on Fridays and until 10:00 p.m. on Thursday
evenings.

[
80
]

Thus, the enactments, in their effects, touch economic interests in a
limited way. No doubt they do so adversely for some persons, but as Dickson,
C.J.C., said in
Edwards Books
(p. 779):

"In interpreting and applying the Charter I believe that
the courts must be cautious to ensure that it does not simply become an
instrument of better situated individuals to roll back legislation which has as
its object the improvement of the condition of less advantaged persons."

[
81
]

For these reasons, we are satisfied that the limitations on the legal
equality rights of those individual retailers who are adversely affected by the
classification of the laws in question are both reasonable and justified.

(c) Conclusion

[
82
]

In light of the foregoing, we have concluded that neither the
Act

nor the bylaw is inconsistent, generally, with the constitution, except as they
infringe the freedom of religion of Saturday-observing retailers, a matter
which may be dealt with under s. 24 by way of appropriate exemption.

[
83
]

It follows that the constitutional challenge to the
Act
and the
bylaw fails in its entirety, and that in the result all the charges are
properly grounded. To the extent the Sunday closing charges were quashed in the
Court of Queen's Bench, the appeal is allowed. Otherwise it is dismissed.

Appeals allowed in part.
